text: Hi, everyone.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm Matt Ragone, and I'm a financial planner at Range.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I want to show you how our financial planners ended up writing the agents that we use every day, and none of us, the financial planners for that matter, write code.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is the build guide, how we did it step-by-step so you can take it back to your own teams, companies, et cetera.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So a quick bit about me, because it matters for how you'll hear this talk.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm not an engineer, I'm a certified financial planner, and I spend my days with clients talking about cashflow, taxes, insurance, retirement, estate, you name it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I also lead the AI adoption for the planning team at Range, which is an all-in-one wealth management company.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Most agent talks you'll hear come from the people who built the platform.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This talk comes from someone on the other side, the people you hand the platform to.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We work in a regulated business.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The output is financial advice to real clients, and the review step is not optional.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this isn't a vendor pitch.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's a method, and it's what actually worked for us.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We started where everyone starts, AI as a chatbot.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'd write a client message, paste it in, and ask it to make it a little clearer or friendlier.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that was useful.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It saved me a few minutes here and there, but I was still doing all of the work manually.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I was just doing it a little bit faster.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The change that actually mattered came later.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Here's what we figured out.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A planner's constraint was never typing speed, for example.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's that we can only be in one place at a time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If I'm on a call with a client, I'm not building someone else's plan.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Writing faster doesn't fix that problem.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What fixes it is work that happens while I'm somewhere else.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So here's what a day looks like now.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm on a call with one client at the same time an agent is drafting a full cash flow analysis or an insurance analysis for a different client.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When the call ends, I open that draft, I fully review it, adjust what needs to be adjusted, and send the client their recommendations.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I want to be really clear about that last step.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The agent doesn't send anything.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A planner reviews every single recommendation before a client sees it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What changed is that the first draft no longer needs me sitting in front of it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Getting there took a lot more than a good prompt, however.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Two things had to be true.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: First, the agent has to work where the work lives, not in a separate chat window I'm copying and pasting it into.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Second, it has to know how we do it, not how financial planning works in general.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The model already knows that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But the agent needs to know how range does it, what we look at first, what we always flag, how we phrase a specific recommendation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That combination is what a skill is, our firm's way of doing one specific piece of work written down so an agent can follow it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The bulk of this talk
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: is how you build one.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Five steps.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Pick, teach, pack, test, and then ship.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: None of them require writing code.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Every one of them requires knowing the work really well, which is exactly why the people doing the work should also be the ones building it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Step one, pick a workflow you repeat.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Your initial instinct is to go for the flashiest work, whatever's taking the most amount of time and the most complex.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Don't.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Pick something you do every week where you already know what good looks like, where you can spot a bad draft at a glance.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Additionally, we recommend choosing some of the least complex workflows to start, but some that require the most manual work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For us, that meant things like cash flow analysis and insurance reviews.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Just for us here at Range, that required the most manual work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And if you can't judge the output quickly, you can't test it and you can't trust it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So look for two things.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You do it often and you know how to judge it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Step two, show it several real cases for previous plans you've delivered.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Take several actual client cases and walk through the work start to finish.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And as you do it, narrate your judgment out loud.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Not just, next I open the pay stub, why you're opening it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What you're looking for.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What would make you stop and ask a question?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That narration is the whole game.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The steps are easy to write down.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The judgment is what makes it your firm's work instead of generic advice.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Step three, pack it into a skill.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A skill isn't just a list of steps.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Two things matter most.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The questions it must ask.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Before it starts, what does it need to know?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What should it confirm with me instead of simply guessing?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the limits it must respect.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What it never does on its own.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In our world, the big one is that it never sends anything to a client.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It drafts, and then a planner decides if it gets sent or needs to be adjusted.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you only write the steps, you get something that simply just runs on its own.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you write the questions and set the limits, you can get something you can trust.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Think of a skill as a recipe.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Once Claude knows how to do the skill, it will repeat your process on command.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Step number four, run it five or 10 times on real cases before anyone else sees it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is the step everyone wants to skip.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Every run teaches you something the skill didn't know yet, an edge case, a question it should have asked, a spot where it sounded confident and was wrong.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You need to fix it, save the skill, and run it again and again and again.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: 5-10 runs sounds like a lot, but it's a lot less work than cleaning up after you hand a half-baked skill to 15, 20, 100 people in your team.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Step 5.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Ship it with an owner and a reviewer.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The owner keeps it current.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Our processes change, tax rules change, and a skill that was right in March can be wrong by December.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The reviewer checks it before the team relies on it, and it's someone other than the author.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Same as a plan.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You don't grade your own work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Once other people depend on a skill, somebody has to be accountable for it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's the difference between a clever personal shortcut and something a team can build on.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So where are we at currently?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Six months in, we have 24 skills across the company and 17 of them are in planning.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And here's the part I didn't expect.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It spread to sales, product, marketing, all without a mandate.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Nobody sent a memo.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: People saw what the planners were doing and started building their own agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Every one of those skills was written and is maintained by planners, marketers, and salespeople, not developers or engineers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A couple of things changed once subject matter experts started building for their own niche.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The skills got a lot more specific.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The person who knows insurance, for example, best builds the insurance skill.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The person who best knows tax, tax code, tax law should be building the tax one.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And a review came naturally.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We already review each other's plans and that's just how planning works.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So now we review each other's skills in that same way.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's the same habit, just a new thing to review.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So why does this matter right now?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Because the bottleneck has moved.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Whether a model can draft a cashflow analysis, that question's already been settled.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It can.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What's not settled, who writes down how your firm does it?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Who tests it before it ships?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Who owns it once 15 other people depend on it?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you're being asked to push agents out past the engineering org, you're about to hit these exact questions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There isn't much field data on this yet, but this is how we've done it here at Range.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So that's it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Thank you so much for listening to this talk.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm Matt Ragone from Range, and you can reach me at mattatrange.com.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Have a great day.
speaker: SPEAKER_00
